title: Resistance & Ohm's Law
description: Resistors, Ohm's law, conductance, resistivity and the power a resistor turns into heat.

study.title: Ohm's law
study.body: A resistor's voltage is proportional to its current: $v = iR$, with $R$ in ohms (Ω). This form assumes the **passive reference configuration** (the current arrow enters the + end). If the current reference enters the − end, write $v = -iR$. Handy unit combinations: V / kΩ = mA and mA × kΩ = V.

study.title: Conductance
study.body: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, measured in siemens (S): $G = 1/R$. Ohm's law then reads $i = Gv$. A large conductance means current flows easily; for example 2 kΩ corresponds to 0.5 mS.

study.title: Resistivity
study.body: The resistance of a uniform conductor grows with its length $L$ and falls with its cross-sectional area $A$. The resistivity $\rho$ (Ω·m) is a material property: copper ≈ $1.72\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m, nichrome (heater wire) ≈ $1.1\times10^{-6}$ Ω·m. For a round wire of diameter $d$, $A = \pi d^2/4$.

study.title: Power in a resistor
study.body: Combining $p = vi$ with Ohm's law gives three equivalent forms. In the passive reference configuration $p \ge 0$ always: a resistor only **absorbs** power and turns it into heat. Real resistors have a **power rating** (e.g. ¼ W); dissipating more than that makes them overheat.

study.title: Open and short circuits
study.body: An **open circuit** is a gap: no current can flow ($i = 0$), whatever the voltage across it — like $R \to \infty$. A **short circuit** is an ideal wire: there is no voltage across it ($v = 0$), whatever current flows — like $R = 0$. All points joined by ideal wires are at the same voltage.

study.title: Worked example
study.body:
A 12 V source is connected across a 2.4 kΩ resistor.
- Current: $i = v/R$ = 12 V / 2.4 kΩ = 5 mA
- Power: $p = v^2/R$ = 144 / 2400 = 0.06 W = 60 mW
- Check: $i^2R$ = (0.005 A)² × 2400 Ω = 60 mW ✓
A ¼ W (250 mW) resistor is safe here.

steps.title: The resistor
steps.body: A resistor limits current and turns electrical energy into heat. Its voltage and current are proportional: double the voltage, double the current. The constant of proportionality is the **resistance** $R$, measured in ohms (Ω).

steps.prompt: A {{V}} V source is connected across a {{R|Ω}} resistor. What current flows?
steps.explanation: The full source voltage is across the resistor. Ohm's law solved for current: $i = v/R$ = {{V}} V / {{R|Ω}} = {{V/R|A}}.

steps.title: Mind the reference directions
steps.body: $v = iR$ holds when the current arrow enters the **+** end of the resistor (passive reference configuration). If the arrow enters the **−** end, Ohm's law picks up a minus sign: $v = -iR$. The physics does not change — only the bookkeeping.

steps.prompt: For this resistor, $v$ is defined + at the top, and $i$ is defined flowing **upward**, into the bottom end. Which equation is correct?
steps.explanation: The arrow enters the resistor at its **−** end, opposite to the passive reference configuration, so $v = -iR$. Check: if real current flows upward (i > 0), it flows from the bottom (higher voltage) to the top, so $v$ (+ at top) is negative — consistent with $v = -iR$.

steps.title: Power in a resistor
steps.body: A resistor absorbs power $p = vi$. Substituting Ohm's law gives two more handy forms. With the passive reference configuration, the power of a resistor is never negative — resistors only absorb energy and turn it into heat.

steps.prompt: A current of {{I|A}} flows through a {{R|Ω}} resistor. How much power does it dissipate?
steps.explanation: $p = i^2R$ = ({{I}} A)² × {{R}} Ω = {{I^2*R|W}}. Square the current in amperes ({{I|A}} = {{I}} A), not in milliamperes!

steps.prompt: A resistor can deliver power to the rest of the circuit if the current through it is negative.
steps.explanation: If $i$ is negative, then $v = iR$ is negative too, so $p = vi = i^2R$ is still positive. A resistor always absorbs power, whatever the direction of the current.

steps.title: Open and short circuits
steps.body:
Two extreme cases appear everywhere:
- **Open circuit**: a break in the path. No current flows ($i = 0$), but any voltage can appear across it. Think $R \to \infty$.
- **Short circuit**: an ideal wire. There is no voltage across it ($v = 0$), but any current can flow. Think $R = 0$.

steps.prompt: Match each element to its defining property
steps.explanation: An open circuit blocks current ($i = 0$, $R \to \infty$); a short circuit has no voltage ($v = 0$, $R = 0$); a resistor sits in between with $v$ proportional to $i$.

steps.prompt: When {{V}} V is applied across a resistor, a current of {{I|A}} flows. What is its resistance?
steps.explanation: $R = v/i$ = {{V}} V / {{I|A}} = {{V}} / {{I}} = {{V/I|Ω}}. Tip: volts divided by milliamperes gives kilo-ohms.

steps.prompt: Conductance $G = 1/R$ is measured in siemens (S). What is the conductance of a {{R|Ω}} resistor?
steps.explanation: $G = 1/R$ = 1 / {{R}} Ω = {{1/R|S}}. Remember 1/kΩ = mS.

steps.prompt: A current of {{I|A}} flows through a {{R|Ω}} resistor (passive reference configuration). What is the voltage across it?
steps.explanation: $v = iR$ = {{I|A}} × {{R|Ω}} = {{I}} A × {{R}} Ω = {{I*R|V}}. Shortcut: mA × kΩ = V.

steps.prompt: How much power does the resistor absorb?
steps.explanation: The resistor has the full {{V}} V across it, so $p = v^2/R$ = ({{V}} V)² / {{R}} Ω = {{V^2}} / {{R}} = {{V^2/R|W}}.

steps.prompt: A {{R|Ω}} resistor has a power rating of {{Pmax}} W. What is the largest voltage you may apply across it?
steps.explanation: From $p = v^2/R$: $v_{max} = \sqrt{P_{max}R}$ = √({{Pmax}} W × {{R}} Ω) = √{{Pmax*R}} = {{sqrt(Pmax*R)|V}}.

steps.prompt: The resistor is {{R|Ω}}. Its voltage $v$ is defined + at the top, and $i$ = {{I|A}} is defined flowing **upward** (into the bottom end). Find $v$.
steps.explanation: The arrow enters the − end, so $v = -iR$ = −{{I|A}} × {{R|Ω}} = {{-I*R|V}}. Current really flows upward through the resistor, from the bottom to the top, so the bottom end is at the higher voltage — that is what the minus sign says.

steps.prompt: A copper wire ($\rho = 1.72\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m) is {{L}} m long and has a diameter of {{d*1000}} mm. What is its resistance?
steps.explanation:
Cross-section: $A = \pi d^2/4$ = π × ({{d}} m)² / 4 = {{pi*d^2/4}} m².
$R = \rho L/A$ = $1.72\times10^{-8}$ × {{L}} / {{pi*d^2/4}} = {{1.72e-8*L/(pi*d^2/4)|Ω}}. Convert mm to m before squaring!

steps.prompt: A wire is replaced by one of the same material that is **twice as long** and has **twice the diameter**. Its resistance…
steps.explanation: $R = \rho L/A$. Doubling $L$ doubles $R$. Doubling the diameter makes the area $\pi d^2/4$ **four** times larger, which divides $R$ by 4. Net factor: 2 / 4 = ½, so the resistance halves.

steps.prompt: Match each quantity to its unit
steps.explanation: Conductance is 1/resistance (S = 1/Ω). Resistivity times length divided by area gives ohms, so resistivity has units Ω·m² / m = Ω·m.

steps.prompt: An electric heater dissipates {{P}} W when connected to {{V}} V. What is its resistance?
A lamp is rated {{P}} W at {{V}} V. Treating it as a constant resistance, how much power does it absorb when operated at {{k*V}} V?
steps.hint: First find the lamp's resistance from its rating.
steps.explanation:
Resistance: $R = V^2/P$ = {{V}}² / {{P}} = {{V^2/P|Ω}}.
At the lower voltage: $p = v^2/R$ = ({{k*V}} V)² / {{V^2/P|Ω}} = {{P*k^2|W}}.
Shortcut: power scales with the **square** of the voltage, $p = P\,(v/V)^2$ = {{P}} × {{k}}² = {{P*k^2|W}}.

steps.prompt: Heater wire is made of nichrome ($\rho = 1.1\times10^{-6}$ Ω·m) with a diameter of {{d*1000}} mm. What length of wire gives a resistance of {{R}} Ω?

A {{L}} m extension cord has two copper conductors (out and back), each with a cross-section of {{A*1e6}} mm² ($\rho = 1.72\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m). A heater draws {{I}} A through it. What voltage is lost across the cord (both conductors together)?
steps.explanation:
One conductor: $R = \rho L/A$ = $1.72\times10^{-8}$ × {{L}} / ({{A*1e6}} × $10^{-6}$) = {{1.72e-8*L/A|Ω}}.
The current goes out through one conductor and back through the other, so the total is $2R$ = {{2*1.72e-8*L/A|Ω}}.
Voltage lost: $v = i \cdot 2R$ = {{I}} A × {{2*1.72e-8*L/A|Ω}} = {{I*2*1.72e-8*L/A|V}}.

steps.prompt: What is the largest current a {{R}} Ω resistor rated at {{P}} W can carry without exceeding its rating?
steps.explanation: From $p = i^2R$: $i_{max} = \sqrt{P/R}$ = √({{P}} W / {{R}} Ω) = {{sqrt(P/R)|A}}.

steps.prompt: An ideal current source of {{I}} A is connected directly across an ideal short circuit (a plain wire). What are the voltage across the wire and the current through it?
steps.explanation: The current source forces {{I}} A around the loop, and the short circuit accepts any current with zero voltage across it. So $i$ = {{I}} A and $v$ = 0 V. Nothing is violated: the source simply delivers zero power ($p = vi = 0$).

steps.prompt: Tap every resistor that carries **no current**.
steps.explanation:
- $R_2$ is bridged by a plain wire (a short circuit), so both of its ends are at the same voltage: $v = 0$ and therefore $i = v/R = 0$. All the current takes the wire.
- $R_4$ is in series with the **open** switch. An open circuit carries no current, so neither does $R_4$.
- The only closed path is $V_s \to R_1 \to$ (wire) $\to R_3$ and back, so $R_1$ and $R_3$ carry the same nonzero current.

steps.prompt: A current of {{I}} A flows through a {{R}} Ω resistor for {{tmin}} minutes. How much heat (energy) does the resistor produce?
